canonical_question: How does the 10% compression ductility at room temperature compare to the ductility expected after exposure to 900 °C, and does embrittlement occur?

question_variants.question: How does the 10% compression ductility at room temperature compare to the ductility expected after exposure to 900 °C, and does embrittlement occur?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The paper reports ~10% compression ductility at room temperature. It does not provide data on ductility after exposure to 900 °C, nor does it explicitly state whether embrittlement occurs after such exposure.

answers.answer: The alloy has reasonable compression ductility (~10%) at room temperature. The provided text does not contain data on ductility or embrittlement after exposure to 900 °C.
answers.boundary_limitation: No data on post-900 °C exposure mechanical properties.
evidence_spans: Figure 1 a shows the XRD pattern of the AlNbTiVZr 0.25 alloy in the initial (annealed at 1200 °C for 24 h) condition.

In the XRD pattern, the Bragg peaks belonging to two phases, namely B2 and Zr 5 Al 3 , were found; the lattice parameters of B2 and Zr 5 Al 3 phases were a = 0.3203 nm and a = 0.7996 nm, c = 0.5374 nm, respectively.

The alloy consisted of two structural constituents: (i) B2 grains (labeled with 1 in Figure 1 b) with the average size of ~80 μm and the chemical composition close to that of the alloy ( Table 1 ) and (ii) light-grey (Zr, Al)-rich particles (labeled with 2 in Figure 1 b; Table 1 ) identified as the Zr 5 Al 3 phase located both along the boundaries of the B2 grains as a discontinuous network and as separate particles or clusters of these particles in the B2 grains interior.
